name: Body of the lateral ventricle
synonyms: central part of the lateral ventricle
function: Central portion posterior to the foramen of Monro and anterior to the atrium, roofed by the corpus callosum. Floor relations include caudate body laterally and thalamus more medially, separated by the stria terminalis/thalamostriate region; fornix and septum pellucidum contribute medially. Choroid plexus lies along the choroidal fissure. This describes gross relationships, not precise boundaries in every specimen.
contextNote: Schematic segment of the committed lateral-ventricular model. The origin and dimensions are display anchors in the atlas frame; segment cut planes and mesh-centroid measurements do not validate boundaries or dimensions in an individual brain. Refer to the complete cast and surrounding anatomical relationships.

efferent: Foramen of Monro → third ventricle; horns/atrium are communicating recesses

bloodSupply: The CSF cavity is not an arterial tissue territory. Body plexus receives mainly lateral posterior choroidal supply with choroidal anastomoses; adjacent caudate/thalamus/callosal tissue receives its own striate, thalamic or callosal arterial supply.

clinical.findings: Central neurocytoma often attaches near the septum pellucidum/foramen region and may obstruct CSF. Calcification and enhancement can support a differential diagnosis but histopathology establishes tumor type.

Tumor or infection can involve the ependymal/subependymal region; abnormal enhancement is nonspecific. Developmental heterotopia and premature-infant germinal-matrix haemorrhage have different mechanisms and should not be treated as the same disorder.
Can accompany upstream CSF obstruction or tissue-volume loss. Aqueductal stenosis typically enlarges lateral/third ventricles; no body shape alone is a specific diagnostic hallmark.
